> **Status.** Working theory note for `forestsearch`. Detailed by design; intended
> to be revised and shortened into an article. Worked Cox and GLM derivations
> appear first (Sections 3–4), then a single general estimation schema (Section 5)
> that subsumes both via the natural-parameter scale of @gao2025.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

`forestsearch` identifies *harm subgroups* in randomized trials by an exhaustive
search over candidate subgroups, retaining those whose estimated treatment
effect is both large and **internally consistent** [@leon2024]. Consistency is
operationalized by repeated sample splitting: a candidate subgroup is split many
times into two random halves, the treatment effect is re-estimated on each half,
and the subgroup is credited each time *both* halves exhibit harm beyond a
threshold. The fraction of consistent splits — the *consistency rate* — must
exceed a cutoff (commonly $0.90$) for the subgroup to be flagged.

The criterion is intuitive and empirically effective, but as defined it is (i)
*computationally expensive*, requiring on the order of $10^3$ refits per
candidate, and (ii) *statistically opaque*: it is not obvious what population
quantity the consistency rate estimates, nor how the $0.90$ cutoff relates to
familiar inferential statements.

This note develops a first-order **resampling representation** of the criterion
with four consequences:

1. **A closed form.** The consistency rate is, to leading order,
   $$
   p_{\mathrm{cons}} \;\approx\; \max\!\Big\{0,\; 2\,\Phi\!\big((\hat\beta - c)/\sigma_D\big) - 1\Big\},
   $$ {#eq-closed}
   where $\hat\beta$ is the subgroup treatment coefficient, $c$ the harm
   threshold on the same scale, $\sigma_D$ the subgroup's robust (sandwich)
   standard error, and $\Phi$ the standard normal CDF. No splitting or refitting
   is required; a single subgroup fit suffices.

2. **A multiplier-bootstrap reading.** The repeated split is a special case of a
   multiplier (wild) bootstrap of the subgroup estimating function. The
   $50/50$ split corresponds to *Rademacher* multipliers; Gaussian multipliers
   recover the score/estimating-function resampling of
   @linweiying1993, @parzenweiying1994 and @jinyingwei2001; centered-Poisson
   multipliers recover the weird/wild survival bootstrap of @dobler2017. All
   share the limit in @eq-closed.

3. **A unified scale.** The representation holds verbatim for the Cox model and
   for generalized linear models because in every case $\hat\beta$ estimates a
   **difference in natural parameters** (DINA) in the sense of @gao2025 — log
   hazard ratio, log odds ratio, log incidence-rate ratio, or mean difference —
   and the per-subject influence contributions are the model's `dfbeta` values.

4. **A calibration.** The $0.90$ cutoff is equivalent to requiring the subgroup
   effect to exceed the harm threshold by $1.645$ robust standard errors, i.e.
   to a one-sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound lying above the threshold
   (@sec-calibration).

The theoretical content is the representation itself: it places an exploratory
heuristic on the same influence-function / multiplier-bootstrap footing as
classical robust survival and GLM inference, and ties the `forestsearch`
*consistency* engine to the *DINA* estimand of @gao2025 already used by the
package's DINA engine.

# The splitting-consistency criterion {#sec-criterion}

Fix a candidate subgroup $S$ with $n_S$ subjects. Let $\theta_S$ denote the
treatment effect for $S$ on a chosen scale (made precise in @sec-schema), and let
$\hat\beta = \hat\beta_S$ be its estimate from a working model fit on $S$
(treatment-only or covariate-adjusted). Write $c$ for the *harm threshold* on the
same scale, oriented so that **harm corresponds to $\hat\beta > c$** (for a
hazard or odds ratio, $c = \log(\text{ratio threshold})$, e.g. $c = \log 1 = 0$;
for a mean or risk difference, $c$ is the difference threshold directly).

The criterion, as implemented, is:

> Draw an independent fair coin $Z_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)$ for each
> subject $i \in S$. Let $A = \{i : Z_i = 1\}$ and $B = S \setminus A$ be the two
> halves. Refit the working model on each half to obtain $\hat\beta^{(A)}$ and
> $\hat\beta^{(B)}$. Call the split **consistent** if $\hat\beta^{(A)} > c$ and
> $\hat\beta^{(B)} > c$. Repeating over many splits, the consistency rate
> $p_{\mathrm{cons}}$ is the proportion of consistent splits; $S$ is flagged if
> $p_{\mathrm{cons}} \ge p^\star$ (e.g. $0.90$).

(Practical implementations impose minimum-size and minimum-event guards on each
half and may use early stopping; these do not change the leading-order analysis
and are discussed in @sec-practice.)

The object of this note is the map $(\hat\beta, S) \mapsto p_{\mathrm{cons}}$.

## Relationship to León et al. (2024), Equation (3) {#sec-leon-eq3}

The closed form @eq-closed is not a departure from the original criterion: it is
the conditional kernel *inside* the identification probability that @leon2024 use
to calibrate the thresholds. In their large-sample Cox approximation the two
half-split log-hazard-ratio estimators are represented as independent normals,
$W_1, W_2 \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(\beta,\, 8/d)$, with $d$ the subgroup
event count, and the probability of *identifying* a subgroup with underlying
log-hazard ratio $\beta$ is their Equation (3),
$$
p(c_1, c_2;\, d, \beta) \;=\; \Pr\!\big(W_1+W_2 \ge 2\log c_1,\ \min(W_1,W_2) \ge \log c_2\big),
$$ {#eq-leon3}
where $c_1 = 1.25$ is the screening threshold and $c_2 = 1.0$ the consistency
threshold. Equation (@eq-leon3) is evaluated by two-dimensional numerical
integration and drives the choice of $(c_1, c_2)$ and the power / type-I
approximations.

Rotate the half-estimators into their average and half-difference,
$$
S := \tfrac12 (W_1 + W_2), \qquad D := \tfrac12 (W_1 - W_2).
$$ {#eq-reparam}
For independent normals of common variance these are themselves independent,
$S \sim N(\beta,\, 4/d)$ and $D \sim N(0,\, 4/d)$, with two readings: $S =
\hat\beta_s$ is the **full-subgroup** estimate and $\operatorname{Var}(S)=4/d$ its
sampling variance, while $D$ is the **split perturbation** with the *same*
variance $\operatorname{Var}(D) = 4/d = \operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_s)$. That the
split perturbation shares the standard error of the full-subgroup estimate is
precisely the identity @eq-sigma-d, here already built into the $8/d$-versus-$4/d$
scaling of (@eq-leon3).

In these coordinates the screening event is $S \ge \log c_1$ and the consistency
event is $\min(W_1,W_2) = S - |D| \ge \log c_2$, i.e. $|D| \le S - \log c_2$.
Because $S \perp D$, (@eq-leon3) factorizes over the screened region as
$$
p(c_1, c_2;\, d, \beta) \;=\; \int_{\log c_1}^{\infty}
  \underbrace{\Big[\,2\Phi\!\Big(\tfrac{s - \log c_2}{\sqrt{4/d}}\Big) - 1\,\Big]}_{\textstyle \text{consistency rate at } \hat\beta = s}
  \; \varphi\!\big(s;\, \beta,\, 4/d\big)\, ds .
$$ {#eq-bridge}
The bracketed factor is exactly the closed form @eq-closed evaluated at
$\hat\beta = s$ (with $c = \log c_2$ and $\sigma_D = \sqrt{4/d}$). Thus **the
consistency rate @eq-closed is the integrand of León's identification
probability**: (@eq-leon3) multiplies it by the screening restriction $S \ge \log
c_1$ and marginalizes it over the sampling density of the subgroup estimate. The
present note isolates that inner factor and conditions on the *observed* estimate
$\hat\beta$ — which is what the per-candidate consistency rate of @leon2024 (their
Step 3(c)) actually computes — whereas (@eq-leon3) is the marginal, design-level
quantity used for threshold calibration.

## An influence-function form of the identification probability {#sec-if-design}

Equation (@eq-bridge) exposes the only model-specific ingredient in León's
identification probability: the variance $4/d$. That value is the large-sample
Cox variance of a treatment-only log-hazard ratio under 1:1 randomization with
$d$ events and *homogeneous* within-subgroup risk-set contributions. Replacing it
with the influence-function (sandwich) variance $\sigma_D^2 = \sum_i \mathrm{db}_i^2$
of @eq-sigma-d gives a design probability that keeps the structure of (@eq-leon3)
but applies verbatim beyond that setting:
$$
p_{\mathrm{IF}}(c_1, c_2;\, \sigma_D^2, \beta) \;=\; \int_{\log c_1}^{\infty}
  \Big[\,2\Phi\!\Big(\tfrac{s - \log c_2}{\sigma_D}\Big) - 1\,\Big]\,
  \varphi\!\big(s;\, \beta,\, \sigma_D^2\big)\, ds .
$$ {#eq-if-design}
When $\sigma_D^2 = 4/d$ this reduces exactly to (@eq-leon3). For a
covariate-adjusted Cox model, unequal allocation, or heterogeneous risk sets,
$\sigma_D^2$ is the robust variance of the adjusted coefficient; for a GLM outcome
it is the dfbeta variance of the natural-parameter (DINA-scale) coefficient of
@sec-glm (log-OR, log-IRR, or mean difference). A single quantity — the
influence-function variance of the subgroup effect — thus carries León's power /
type-I machinery from the Cox model to the general-response schema of @sec-schema,
and since $\sigma_D^2$ is read from one fitted model, (@eq-if-design) is as cheap
to evaluate as (@eq-leon3).

For **power**, (@eq-if-design) is evaluated at the true subgroup's $\beta =
\log\theta^\dagger(H)$ and its $\sigma_D^2$; for the **per-candidate type-I rate**,
at the null value (e.g. $\beta = \log\theta^\dagger(\mathrm{ITT}) \le 0$ under a
uniformly beneficial treatment). Both are single-subgroup probabilities, and for
power — where the target $H$ is one specific subgroup — that is the right object.

**False discovery is a different and harder object, and the variance substitution
alone does not resolve it.** The search flags a subgroup when *any* of the $S$
overlapping candidates passes screening and consistency (or selects the
maximally-consistent one), so the search-level false-discovery probability is a
union over a strongly correlated family,
$$
\Pr\!\Big(\textstyle\bigcup_{g=1}^{S}
   \big\{\hat\beta_g \ge \log c_1,\ |D_g| \le \hat\beta_g - \log c_2\big\}\ \Big|\ H_0\Big),
$$ {#eq-fdr}
not a single-subgroup probability. A per-candidate calculation such as
(@eq-leon3) or (@eq-if-design) necessarily under-states (@eq-fdr) because it omits
the multiplicity and the overlap among candidates — the practical reason
search-level false discovery has resisted approximation from the per-subgroup
formula.

The influence-function representation is, however, exactly what (@eq-fdr)
requires, because it supplies the *joint* law that (@eq-leon3) cannot. Each
candidate satisfies $\hat\beta_g - \beta_g \approx \sum_i \mathrm{db}_{g,i}$ and has
a split perturbation $D_g = \sum_i G_i\,\mathrm{db}_{g,i}$ driven by the **same**
multiplier vector $G$, so the cross-candidate covariances
$\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_g, \hat\beta_{g'}) = \sum_i \mathrm{db}_{g,i}\,\mathrm{db}_{g',i}$
follow from the shared $N \times S$ influence matrix. This makes (@eq-fdr)
approximable by a **multiplier bootstrap over the whole candidate family**: draw
one $G^{(b)}$, propagate it to every candidate's $(\hat\beta_g,\, D_g^{(b)})$
through the influence matrix, apply the screening-and-consistency rule to each,
and record whether any candidate passes (or what the selection rule returns); the
empirical frequency over draws estimates (@eq-fdr) with the correct correlation
structure, at the cost of one pass over the influence matrix per draw rather than
a re-fit. That is a development beyond a variance swap and a natural next step —
but the per-candidate revision (@eq-if-design) and the family-level extension
share the same ingredient, the per-subject influence contributions.

# The Cox survival case {#sec-cox}

We first treat the time-to-event setting in full, then mirror it for GLMs in
@sec-glm and unify in @sec-schema.

## Model and estimator

On subgroup $S$, observations are $(Y_i^c, \Delta_i, Z_i^{\mathrm{trt}}, X_i)$,
with $Y_i^c$ the observed time, $\Delta_i$ the event indicator,
$Z_i^{\mathrm{trt}} \in \{0,1\}$ treatment, and $X_i$ optional adjustment
covariates. Under proportional hazards [@cox1972],
$$
\lambda_i(t) \;=\; \lambda_0(t)\,\exp\!\big(\beta\, Z_i^{\mathrm{trt}} + \gamma^\top X_i\big),
$$
the estimand is the subgroup **log hazard ratio** $\theta_S = \beta$, estimated
by the partial-likelihood maximizer $\hat\beta$ solving the score equation
$$
U(\beta,\hat\gamma) \;=\; \sum_{i \in S} U_i(\hat\beta,\hat\gamma) \;=\; 0,
$$ {#eq-coxscore}
where $U_i$ is subject $i$'s contribution to the partial-likelihood score for
the treatment coefficient (after profiling the baseline hazard and, if present,
the nuisance coefficient $\gamma$).

## Per-subject influence (dfbeta)

Let $\mathcal{I}$ be the observed partial-likelihood information for $\beta$. The
infinitesimal-jackknife / case-deletion influence of subject $i$ on $\hat\beta$
is the **dfbeta**
$$
\mathrm{db}_i \;\equiv\; \mathcal{I}^{-1} U_i(\hat\beta,\hat\gamma)
\;\approx\; \hat\beta - \hat\beta_{(-i)},
$$ {#eq-coxdfbeta}
returned directly by `residuals(coxph_fit, type = "dfbeta")` (treatment column).
These are the building blocks of the @linwei1989 robust ("sandwich") variance:
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{rob}}(\hat\beta) \;=\; \sum_{i \in S} \mathrm{db}_i^2 .
$$ {#eq-coxrobvar}

## The split, linearized

Encode a split by inclusion indicators $Z_i \in \{0,1\}$ and write the
half-sample estimator $\hat\beta^{(A)}$ as the solution of the *weighted* score
$\sum_{i} Z_i\, U_i(\beta) = 0$. A first-order expansion about $\hat\beta$, using
$\sum_i Z_i\,\dot U_i \approx \tfrac12 \sum_i \dot U_i = -\tfrac12 \mathcal{I}$
(each half carries about half the information), gives
$$
\hat\beta^{(A)} - \hat\beta
\;\approx\; \mathcal{I}^{-1}\!\!\sum_{i \in S} \big(Z_i - \tfrac12\big) U_i(\hat\beta)
\;=\; \sum_{i \in S} G_i\, \mathrm{db}_i \;=:\; D,
\qquad G_i := 2Z_i - 1 .
$$ {#eq-coxlin}
Here we used $\sum_i U_i(\hat\beta) = 0$ from @eq-coxscore, so only the *centered*
indicators $Z_i - \tfrac12 = G_i/2$ survive, and $\mathcal{I}^{-1}U_i = \mathrm{db}_i$.
The complementary half $B$ uses indicators $1 - Z_i$, i.e. multipliers $-G_i$, so
$$
\hat\beta^{(B)} - \hat\beta \;\approx\; -\,D .
$$ {#eq-coxmirror}

**The two halves are mirror images of the full-sample estimate**, perturbed by
the same $D$. The $G_i = 2Z_i - 1 \in \{-1,+1\}$ are independent **Rademacher**
multipliers (mean $0$, variance $1$): the fair-coin split *is* a Rademacher
multiplier bootstrap of the subgroup score.

## Consistency event and closed form

Because $\hat\beta^{(A)} \approx \hat\beta + D$ and $\hat\beta^{(B)} \approx
\hat\beta - D$ (relabeling the sign of $D$ is immaterial), both halves exceed $c$
iff the smaller one does:
$$
\{\hat\beta^{(A)} > c\} \cap \{\hat\beta^{(B)} > c\}
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
\hat\beta - |D| > c
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
|D| < \hat\beta - c .
$$ {#eq-event}
The split perturbation $D = \sum_i G_i\,\mathrm{db}_i$ is a sum of $n_S$
independent mean-zero terms with
$$
\sigma_D^2 \;:=\; \mathrm{Var}(D \mid \text{data}) \;=\; \sum_{i \in S} \mathrm{db}_i^2
\;=\; \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{rob}}(\hat\beta),
$$ {#eq-sigma-d}
so by @eq-coxrobvar **the standard deviation of the split perturbation equals the
robust standard error of $\hat\beta$.** A central limit theorem in $n_S$ gives
$D \mid \text{data} \approx \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_D^2)$, and @eq-event yields the
closed form

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Proposition 1 (closed-form consistency rate).**
Under the linearization @eq-coxlin and asymptotic normality of $D$,
$$
p_{\mathrm{cons}}
\;=\; \Pr\big(|D| < \hat\beta - c\big)
\;\approx\; \max\!\Big\{0,\; 2\,\Phi\!\big((\hat\beta - c)/\sigma_D\big) - 1\Big\}.
$$
:::

*Proof sketch.* For $\hat\beta > c$, $\Pr(|D| < \hat\beta - c) =
\Phi(\tfrac{\hat\beta-c}{\sigma_D}) - \Phi(-\tfrac{\hat\beta-c}{\sigma_D}) =
2\Phi(\tfrac{\hat\beta-c}{\sigma_D}) - 1$; for $\hat\beta \le c$ the probability
is $0$. $\square$

A Monte Carlo version draws multiplier vectors $G^{(b)}$, forms $D^{(b)} =
\sum_i G_i^{(b)}\mathrm{db}_i$, and averages $\mathbf 1\{|D^{(b)}| < \hat\beta -
c\}$; @eq-closed is its analytic limit and the two agree to simulation error.

## Relationship to existing survival resampling

@eq-coxlin is exactly the **resampled estimating function** of
@parzenweiying1994 and the **perturbed minimand** of @jinyingwei2001 specialized
to the Cox score, and the Gaussian-multiplier instance is the martingale-residual
simulation of @linweiying1993. The role of $\sum_i \mathrm{db}_i^2$ as the
sampling variance of $\hat\beta$ is the robust-variance result of @linwei1989.
What is specific here is the *direction of use*: rather than resampling to obtain
a confidence region for $\hat\beta$, we read off the probability that a
$50/50$-split pair *both* lands on the harm side of $c$ — and recognize this as a
tail functional of the same multiplier-bootstrap law.

# The generalized linear model case {#sec-glm}

The GLM development is the exact analogue, with the partial-likelihood score
replaced by the GLM score and `dfbeta` computed from the GLM fit.

## Models and estimands

On $S$, fit a working GLM $g\big(\mathbb E[Y_i \mid Z_i^{\mathrm{trt}}, X_i]\big)
= \beta Z_i^{\mathrm{trt}} + \gamma^\top X_i$ with link $g$ matched to the effect
measure:

| Response | Model / link | $\hat\beta$ estimates | Scale of $c$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| binary | logistic ($\mathrm{logit}$) | log odds ratio | $\log(\text{OR})$ |
| binary | log-binomial / mod. Poisson | log relative risk | $\log(\text{RR})$ |
| binary | identity-binomial | risk difference | identity |
| continuous | linear (identity) | mean difference | identity |
| count / rate | Poisson + $\log$-offset | log incidence-rate ratio | $\log(\text{IRR})$ |

: GLM working models and the scale of the harm threshold $c$. {#tbl-glm}

For the canonical-link families the score contribution for $\beta$ is
$$
U_i(\beta,\gamma) \;=\; Z_i^{\mathrm{trt}}\big(Y_i - \mu_i\big),
\qquad \mu_i = g^{-1}\!\big(\beta Z_i^{\mathrm{trt}} + \gamma^\top X_i\big),
$$ {#eq-glmscore}
and the Fisher information is $\mathcal{I} = \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{W}
\mathbf{X}$ with weights $\mathbf{W}$. The case-deletion influence is the GLM
**dfbeta**
$$
\mathrm{db}_i \;\approx\; \big(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}\big)^{-1}_{\,\beta\beta\text{-row}}\,
x_i\,(Y_i - \mu_i),
$$ {#eq-glmdfbeta}
the treatment column of `stats::dfbeta(glm_fit)`, with $\sum_i \mathrm{db}_i^2$
the Huber–White [@white1980] / infinitesimal-jackknife [@efron1982] robust
variance of $\hat\beta$.

## The split, linearized

The derivation of @sec-cox transfers without change: the half-sample GLM
coefficient solves $\sum_i Z_i U_i(\beta) = 0$, and the identical first-order
expansion (using $\sum_i U_i(\hat\beta)=0$ and $\sum_i Z_i \dot U_i \approx
\tfrac12 \mathcal I$) gives
$$
\hat\beta^{(A)} - \hat\beta \;\approx\; \sum_{i\in S} G_i\,\mathrm{db}_i = D,
\qquad
\hat\beta^{(B)} - \hat\beta \;\approx\; -D,
\qquad
\sigma_D^2 = \sum_{i\in S}\mathrm{db}_i^2 .
$$ {#eq-glmlin}
Proposition 1 therefore holds verbatim, with $c$ taken from @tbl-glm
($c=\log(\text{threshold})$ for ratio measures, $c=\text{threshold}$ for identity
measures). The linear (mean-difference) case is essentially exact rather than
first-order, since ordinary least squares is linear in $Y$ and the half-sample
coefficient is an exact linear functional of the responses; the
logistic/Poisson cases are first-order as in Cox.

## When the representation does not apply

The argument requires $\hat\beta$ to be a *single coefficient* of a converged
working model with a well-defined influence function. It therefore does **not**
cover (i) the incidence-rate *difference* (a delta-method contrast, not a
coefficient), (ii) effects defined through propensity weighting or
G-computation, where the estimand is not a single fitted coefficient, and (iii)
non-convergent fits (e.g. separation in identity-link binomial). In these cases
the closed form is unavailable and one falls back to literal splitting
(@sec-practice).

# A general estimation schema via natural parameters {#sec-schema}

Sections 3–4 are two instances of one structure. We now state it abstractly,
using the **difference-in-natural-parameters (DINA)** estimand of @gao2025 as the
unifying scale, and show why the same resampling representation governs both.

## DINA as the common scale

@gao2025 argue that for general responses the natural object of heterogeneous
treatment-effect analysis is not the difference in conditional means (CATE) but
the **difference in natural parameters**,
$$
\tau(x) \;=\; \eta_1(x) - \eta_0(x), \qquad \eta_w(x) = g\big(\mathbb E[Y(w)\mid X=x]\big),
$$ {#eq-dina}
where $g$ is the canonical link of the response's exponential family (Gaussian,
Bernoulli, Poisson) or the log-hazard transform for the Cox model. Concretely,
DINA is the **mean difference** (Gaussian), the **log odds ratio** (Bernoulli),
the **log incidence-rate ratio** (Poisson), and the **log hazard ratio** (Cox).
These are precisely the four effect measures of @tbl-glm together with the Cox
case of @sec-cox.

Two properties of @eq-dina motivate doing subgroup consistency on this scale.
First, natural parameters are unconstrained on $\mathbb R$, so covariate effects
on the treatment effect are modeled without the support constraints that distort
risk differences. Second — the CRASH-3 illustration of @gao2025 — heterogeneity
is often *simpler* (closer to linear) on the natural-parameter scale than on the
mean / risk-difference scale, so a subgroup of constant DINA is a more natural
target than a subgroup of constant risk difference.

## The schema

For a candidate subgroup $S$, take the indicator basis $z(x)=\mathbf 1\{x\in S\}$
in the @gao2025 representation $\tau(x)=z(x)^\top\beta$, so that $\beta_S$ is the
subgroup's (constant) DINA. The schema has three ingredients:

1. **Estimand.** $\theta_S = \beta_S$, the subgroup DINA on the natural-parameter
   scale (@eq-dina).

2. **Estimator.** Any asymptotically linear estimator $\hat\beta_S$ of $\beta_S$
   with computable per-subject influence contributions $\mathrm{db}_i$ such that
   $\hat\beta_S - \beta_S \approx \sum_{i\in S}\mathrm{db}_i$ and
   $\sum_i \mathrm{db}_i^2 \to \mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_S)$.

3. **Consistency map.** The $50/50$ split perturbs $\hat\beta_S$ by
   $D=\sum_i G_i\,\mathrm{db}_i$ with Rademacher $G_i$, giving the half-sample
   mirror pair $\hat\beta_S \pm D$ and the closed-form rate of Proposition 1,
   $$
   p_{\mathrm{cons}} \approx \max\{0,\,2\Phi((\hat\beta_S - c)/\sigma_D)-1\},
   \qquad \sigma_D = \Big(\textstyle\sum_i \mathrm{db}_i^2\Big)^{1/2}.
   $$

The Cox and GLM cases differ *only* in ingredient 2 — the link $g$, the
likelihood (partial vs full), and how $\mathrm{db}_i$ is computed (score
residuals vs `dfbeta`). Ingredients 1 and 3 are identical, which is why
Proposition 1 is stated once and specialized twice.

## Choice of estimator within the schema

The schema is agnostic to *which* DINA estimator occupies ingredient 2.

* **Working-model coefficient (current `forestsearch`).** The within-subgroup
  partial-likelihood / GLM coefficient, optionally covariate-adjusted. Here
  $\mathrm{db}_i$ is exactly the model `dfbeta`, and the development of
  Sections 3–4 applies directly. This is the estimator behind the closed form
  used in the package.

* **Orthogonalized DINA-learner (@gao2025).** The R-learner-style
  [@robinson1988; @niewager2021] estimator that plugs cross-fitted nuisance
  functions $\hat a(x)$ (a variance-weighted propensity) and $\hat\nu(x)$ (a
  natural-parameter baseline) into a one-parameter likelihood for $\beta_S$. By
  Neyman orthogonality the influence of the nuisance estimates is
  asymptotically negligible, so $\hat\beta_S$ is again asymptotically linear and
  the schema applies with $\mathrm{db}_i$ replaced by the *orthogonalized*
  influence contributions. This is the natural route to a consistency rate that
  is robust to confounding in observational data, and it connects the package's
  *consistency* engine to its *DINA* engine on a common footing.

* **Quasi-likelihood.** @gao2025 note the DINA construction extends to
  quasi-likelihoods (mean–variance specifications) for overdispersion; the
  schema inherits this, with $\mathrm{db}_i$ from the quasi-score.

In all three, the consistency rate is the same tail functional of a
multiplier-bootstrap law; only the influence contributions change.

# Multiplier-bootstrap equivalences {#sec-multiplier}

The closed form depends on the multiplier law only through its first two moments
($\mathbb E G_i = 0$, $\mathrm{Var}\,G_i = 1$). Three choices coincide in the
limit @eq-closed:

| Multiplier $G_i$ | Distribution | Recovers |
|---|---|---|
| $2Z_i - 1$, $Z_i\sim\mathrm{Ber}(1/2)$ | Rademacher $\pm 1$ | the literal $50/50$ split |
| $G_i \sim \mathcal N(0,1)$ | Gaussian | score/estimating-function resampling [@linweiying1993; @parzenweiying1994; @jinyingwei2001] |
| $G_i \sim \mathrm{Pois}(1) - 1$ | centered Poisson | weird/wild survival bootstrap [@dobler2017] |

: Multiplier laws giving the same limiting consistency rate. {#tbl-mult}

Thus the León *et al.* split, Lin-type Gaussian resampling, and the
Dobler–Beyersmann–Pauly weird bootstrap are three coordinates on one object: a
multiplier (exchangeably weighted) bootstrap of the subgroup estimating function
[@praestgaardwellner1993]. The split is distinguished only by being the *finite*
Rademacher member that the original algorithm realizes by literal subsetting. The
closed form is the common Gaussian-limit value; the Monte Carlo rate under any of
the three laws converges to it.

# Calibration and interpretation {#sec-calibration}

Inverting Proposition 1 gives the cutoff calibration. The subgroup passes the
consistency screen at level $p^\star$ iff
$$
2\Phi\!\big((\hat\beta - c)/\sigma_D\big) - 1 \ge p^\star
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
\frac{\hat\beta - c}{\sigma_D} \;\ge\; z_{(1+p^\star)/2},
$$ {#eq-calib}
i.e.
$$
\hat\beta - z_{(1+p^\star)/2}\,\sigma_D \;\ge\; c .
$$ {#eq-calib2}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Corollary (confidence-bound reading).**
The consistency screen at level $p^\star$ is exactly the requirement that the
*one-sided $(1+p^\star)/2$ robust lower confidence bound* for the subgroup effect
lie above the harm threshold $c$.
:::

For the default $p^\star = 0.90$, $(1+p^\star)/2 = 0.95$ and $z_{0.95}=1.645$:
**a $90\%$ consistency rate is equivalent to the subgroup effect exceeding the
harm threshold by at least $1.645$ robust standard errors** — a one-sided $95\%$
lower bound above threshold. This turns an opaque cutoff into a transparent
inferential statement and exposes the screen's operating characteristics: it is a
$z$-test of $H_0: \beta_S \le c$ at one-sided level $1-(1+p^\star)/2$, evaluated
with the robust (split-matched) standard error $\sigma_D$.

Two practical reads follow. First, the screen tightens with subgroup size only
through $\sigma_D$; small subgroups have large $\sigma_D$ and must show a larger
$\hat\beta - c$ to pass. Second, choosing $p^\star$ is choosing a one-sided
confidence level, which can be set to a target false-positive rate rather than by
convention.

# Numerical validation {#sec-validation}

The closed form has been checked against the literal split on real and simulated
data.

* **Cox / GBSG.** On the published GBSG harm subgroup
  ($\hat\beta$ corresponding to $\mathrm{HR}=1.95$), the literal-split
  consistency rate ($0.951$) is reproduced by @eq-closed to the third decimal,
  and the candidate ranking is preserved across the search.

* **GLM grids.** Across simulated odds-ratio, mean-difference and
  incidence-rate-ratio scenarios (unadjusted and covariate-adjusted), the mean
  absolute error of @eq-closed against the literal split is $\approx 0.02$ (OR),
  $\approx 0.003$ (MD; near-exact, per the OLS linearity above), and
  $\approx 0.003$ (IRR), with the largest discrepancies in the small-$n_S$,
  intermediate-rate regime where the normal approximation to $D$ is weakest.

* **Applied (ACTG175 binary/OR).** Re-running a full search under literal
  splitting and under the closed form selects the identical subgroup with
  per-candidate rates agreeing to the displayed precision.

The error pattern matches the theory: exact in the linear case, first-order
elsewhere, and degrading where $n_S$ is small enough that $D$ is not yet
Gaussian.

An illustrative computation (not evaluated here) from a fitted model:

```r
# Cox
db <- residuals(coxph_fit, type = "dfbeta")[, "treat"]
beta <- coef(coxph_fit)[["treat"]]; sigma_D <- sqrt(sum(db^2))
c_thr <- log(1)  # HR > 1 = harm
p_cons <- max(0, 2 * pnorm((beta - c_thr) / sigma_D) - 1)

# GLM (e.g. logistic / log-OR)
db <- stats::dfbeta(glm_fit)[, "treat"]
beta <- coef(glm_fit)[["treat"]]; sigma_D <- sqrt(sum(db^2))
c_thr <- log(1)  # OR > 1 = harm
p_cons <- max(0, 2 * pnorm((beta - c_thr) / sigma_D) - 1)
```

# Practical considerations {#sec-practice}

**Minimum-size and event guards.** Implementations require each half to meet
minimum sample-size and event counts; these truncate the multiplier support
slightly but do not alter the leading-order law. They mainly matter in the
small-$n_S$ regime where the approximation is already loosest.

**Early stopping / two-stage screening.** The literal algorithm's two-stage
early stopping exists only to *limit the number of refits*; the closed form
needs none, so when the resampling representation is used the two-stage machinery
is bypassed and the rate is read from a single fit.

**Fallback.** When ingredient 2 is unavailable (incidence-rate difference,
propensity/G-computation effects, or a non-convergent candidate fit;
@sec-glm), the implementation reverts to literal splitting for that candidate, so
a rate is always produced.

**Across-candidate stopping.** A separate early-stop that halts the candidate
loop once a sufficiently consistent subgroup is found is orthogonal to the
within-candidate computation and is unaffected.

**Cost.** The representation replaces $O(10^3)$ refits per candidate by one fit
plus an $O(n_S)$ reduction. The wall-clock benefit is masked when candidate
evaluation is already parallelized, but compounds inside resampling procedures
(e.g. the post-selection bootstrap) where each replicate re-runs the search
sequentially.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

The splitting-consistency criterion of @leon2024 was introduced as an
exploratory device. The representation here shows it is, to first order, a
recognizable statistical object — a multiplier-bootstrap tail probability of the
subgroup estimating function — with a closed form @eq-closed, a robust-SE scale
@eq-sigma-d, and a confidence-bound calibration @eq-calib2. The same statement
covers the Cox model and generalized linear models because both estimate a
difference in natural parameters in the sense of @gao2025; the response type
enters only through the link and the influence contributions.

Several threads follow. The schema's ingredient 2 invites the orthogonalized
DINA-learner as a confounding-robust estimator for observational settings,
unifying the package's consistency and DINA engines. The multiplier
equivalences (@tbl-mult) suggest that the choice of resampling law is a modeling
convenience rather than a substantive one, and that variance-stabilizing or
studentized multipliers might sharpen the small-$n_S$ approximation. Finally, the
confidence-bound reading of the cutoff (@sec-calibration) makes the screen's
false-positive behavior explicit and, in principle, calibratable to a target
rate rather than to convention.

The main limitations are the leading-order nature of the expansion (exact only in
the linear/MD case) and its reliance on a single-coefficient, converged estimator;
both are visible in the small-$n_S$ tail of the validation and are handled in
practice by the literal-split fallback.

# Appendix: A family-level FDR routine (prototype) {#sec-appendix-fdr}

This appendix gives a runnable prototype of the family-level false-discovery
calculation of @sec-if-design (Equation @eq-fdr): a multiplier bootstrap over the
*whole* candidate family that reuses the per-subject influence contributions
rather than refitting on simulated null data. The same code is provided as the
standalone script `fdr_family_multiplier.R`, which adds a self-contained
simulated-null demonstration (`run_fdr_family_demo()`); the version below carries
condensed comments.

The inputs are an $N \times S$ influence matrix $\mathbf{B}$ (column $g$ is
candidate $g$'s treatment-coefficient `dfbeta`, zero for subjects outside $g$),
the observed candidate estimates, and the screening/consistency thresholds. A
candidate is flagged when $\hat\beta_g \ge t_g$ with $t_g =
\max(c_{\mathrm{screen}},\, c_{\mathrm{cons}} + z\,\sigma_{D,g})$ and
$z = \Phi^{-1}((1+p^\star)/2)$. Per draw, one shared multiplier vector is
propagated to *all* candidates through $\mathbf{B}$ (a single matrix product), so
candidate overlap — the cross-candidate correlation $\sum_i \mathrm{db}_{g,i}
\mathrm{db}_{g',i}$ — is respected exactly; the family discovery probability is the
fraction of draws in which any candidate is flagged.

```r
# Mean-zero, unit-variance multipliers (Rademacher = the 50/50 split).
.draw_multipliers <- function(n, draws, type = c("rademacher", "gaussian", "poisson")) {
  type <- match.arg(type)
  g <- switch(type,
    rademacher = sample(c(-1, 1), n * draws, replace = TRUE),
    gaussian   = stats::rnorm(n * draws),
    poisson    = stats::rpois(n * draws, 1) - 1)   # centred Poisson: mean 0, var 1
  matrix(g, nrow = n, ncol = draws)
}

# Build the N x S influence matrix: column g = candidate g's treatment dfbeta,
# placed at its members' rows, zero elsewhere.  candidates[[g]] = list(idx, dfbeta).
assemble_influence <- function(candidates, N) {
  B <- matrix(0, nrow = N, ncol = length(candidates))
  for (g in seq_along(candidates)) {
    cg <- candidates[[g]]
    B[cg$idx, g] <- cg$dfbeta
  }
  B
}

# Family-level false-discovery (type-I) probability by multiplier bootstrap.
# Flag rule (per candidate): beta*_g >= t_g, with the family centred at beta_null
# (uniform-benefit / boundary null) for the type-I calculation.
fdr_family_multiplier <- function(influence, beta_hat, sigma_D = NULL,
                                  c_screen, c_consistency = 0, p_star = 0.90,
                                  beta_null = 0, center = c("null", "observed"),
                                  draws = 2000L,
                                  multiplier = c("rademacher", "gaussian", "poisson"),
                                  seed = NULL) {
  center <- match.arg(center); multiplier <- match.arg(multiplier)
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)
  influence <- as.matrix(influence); N <- nrow(influence); S <- ncol(influence)
  if (is.null(sigma_D)) sigma_D <- sqrt(colSums(influence^2))
  if (length(beta_null) == 1L) beta_null <- rep(beta_null, S)

  z   <- stats::qnorm((1 + p_star) / 2)
  t_g <- pmax(c_screen, c_consistency + z * sigma_D)        # per-candidate flag threshold
  centre <- if (center == "null") beta_null else beta_hat

  Xi <- .draw_multipliers(N, draws, multiplier)             # N x draws
  P  <- crossprod(influence, Xi)                            # S x draws : one matvec, all candidates
  beta_star <- centre + P                                   # recycles `centre`/`t_g` down columns
  num_flag  <- colSums(beta_star >= t_g)

  marginal <- stats::pnorm((t_g - beta_null) / sigma_D, lower.tail = FALSE)
  list(fdr                = mean(num_flag > 0L),            # search-level false-discovery prob
       e_num_flagged      = mean(num_flag),
       marginal           = marginal,                       # per-candidate (independent) probs
       union_independent  = 1 - prod(1 - marginal),         # independence bound, for contrast
       thresholds         = t_g,
       n_observed_flagged = sum(beta_hat >= t_g))
}
```

Wiring it to a fitted search: for each candidate subgroup, collect its member row
indices and the treatment-coefficient `dfbeta` (Cox: `residuals(fit, type =
"dfbeta")[, treat]`; GLM: `stats::dfbeta(fit)[, treat]`), then call the routine.

```r
candidates <- lapply(fs_candidates, function(cg)
  list(idx = cg$member_rows, dfbeta = cg$treat_dfbeta))
B   <- assemble_influence(candidates, N = nrow(analysis_data))
out <- fdr_family_multiplier(
  influence = B, beta_hat = vapply(fs_candidates, `[[`, numeric(1), "beta"),
  c_screen = log(1.25), c_consistency = log(1.0), p_star = 0.90,
  beta_null = log(itt_or), draws = 4000, multiplier = "rademacher")
out$fdr               # search-level false-discovery probability
out$union_independent # naive independence bound (for contrast)
```

On a simulated null with a homogeneous protective effect (no harm subgroup), the
routine returns a family false-discovery probability well above any single
candidate's marginal — the multiplicity that the per-candidate probability
(@eq-leon3) misses — yet below the independence union bound, since overlapping
candidates are positively correlated and false flags cluster rather than
multiply. This is the natural next step toward replacing the per-candidate
type-I/FDR approximation with one that accounts for the full search.
